stem: On what date was the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) founded?

options.rationale: Correct: celebrated as Africa Day.

options.content: 9 July 2002
options.rationale: This is the date on which the African Union was launched.

options.content: 24 October 1945
options.rationale: This is the date on which the UN Charter came into force.

options.content: 18 April 1980
options.rationale: This is the date of Zimbabwe's independence.

explanation: The OAU Charter was signed at Addis Ababa on 25 May 1963.

stem: What was the main task of the OAU Liberation Committee?

options.content: To support liberation movements fighting colonial and white-minority rule
options.rationale: Correct: it gave money, training and arms.

options.content: To organise elections in every independent African state each year
options.rationale: It did not run elections.

options.content: To control trade between African states and the countries of Europe
options.rationale: It did not control trade.

options.content: To command a standing African army that kept order in every country
options.rationale: The OAU had no standing army.

explanation: The Liberation Committee, based in Dar es Salaam, channelled funds, training and arms to liberation movements.

stem: In which city was the African Union launched in July 2002?

options.content: Lomé
options.rationale: The Constitutive Act was adopted at Lomé in 2000.

options.content: Durban
options.rationale: Correct: South Africa's President chaired the first Assembly.

options.content: Sirte
options.rationale: The Sirte Declaration of 1999 called for a union.

options.content: Dar es Salaam
options.rationale: This was the base of the Liberation Committee.

explanation: The AU was launched at Durban on 9 July 2002; the Constitutive Act had been adopted at Lomé in 2000.

stem: How did the principle of intervention in the AU differ from that of the OAU?

options.content: The AU forbids all intervention in every single case, while the OAU always intervened in other states
options.rationale: The OAU stressed non-interference.

options.content: The AU and OAU both allowed any member state to attack any other member state
options.rationale: Neither organisation allowed this.

options.content: The AU may intervene in grave cases such as genocide; the OAU stressed non-interference
options.rationale: Correct: this is Article 4(h) of the Constitutive Act.

options.content: The AU lets non-African states decide when and where Africans should intervene
options.rationale: The decision belongs to the AU.

explanation: Article 4(h) of the Constitutive Act gives the AU the right to intervene in grave circumstances; the OAU's central principle was non-interference.
hints: Think of the Constitutive Act and genocide.

stem: What did the Cairo Declaration of 1964 decide about the colonial borders of Africa?

options.content: That all borders should be redrawn according to the language of each people
options.rationale: It confirmed the existing borders.

options.content: That Europe should draw new borders for Africa by treaty
options.rationale: That was the aim of the nineteenth-century partition.

options.content: That states should respect the borders they inherited at independence
options.rationale: Correct: the aim was to avoid border wars.

options.content: That the borders of Africa should be abolished on the same day
options.rationale: This did not happen.

explanation: The Cairo Declaration confirmed the principle of respecting the borders inherited at independence, although they were drawn by colonial powers.
hints: Think of the OAU's wish to avoid border wars.

stem: Which was a major weakness of the OAU?

options.content: It had too many soldiers and used them to rule member states by force
options.rationale: It had no soldiers.

options.content: It refused to support any liberation movement in southern Africa at any time
options.rationale: It supported several.

options.content: It enforced every decision with sanctions against its own members and their leaders
options.rationale: Its decisions were not binding.

options.content: It had no armed force, and non-interference limited its action
options.rationale: Correct: it could not act against internal abuse.

explanation: The OAU lacked force and money, and its non-interference principle meant it did not act when governments mistreated their people.

stem: Which pairing of body and its role is correct?

options.content: Pan-African Parliament: the AU organ that commands the African military forces
options.rationale: It is a parliamentary organ, not a command.

options.content: Peace and Security Council: handles conflict prevention and peace operations
options.rationale: Correct: operational from 2004.

options.content: African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights: the body that sets the AU's budget
options.rationale: It is a court.

options.content: Liberation Committee: the AU organ that supports the African Union's anti-piracy force
options.rationale: It was an OAU body.

explanation: The Peace and Security Council, operational from 2004, handles conflict prevention and peace operations.
hints: Match each organ with its function.

stem: Which point best supports the view that the AU is more effective than the OAU?

options.content: It meets once a year at a summit of leaders, as the OAU did
options.rationale: This shows similarity, not greater effect.

options.content: It has its headquarters in Addis Ababa, as the OAU had before it
options.rationale: This shows continuity.

options.content: It depends on outside funding for much of its programme of work
options.rationale: This is a weakness.

options.content: It has sent peace operations and suspended governments after coups
options.rationale: Correct: it has acted where the OAU rarely did.

explanation: The AU has deployed peace operations (for example in Burundi, Darfur and Somalia) and has suspended governments after coups, which the OAU seldom did.
hints: Look for evidence of new action.

stem: Describe the aims of the OAU.

points.description: To promote the unity and solidarity of African states
To co-ordinate and intensify co-operation for development
To defend the sovereignty and territorial integrity of members
To eradicate colonialism from Africa and promote international co-operation

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The OAU aimed to promote the unity and solidarity of African states and to co-ordinate their co-operation for development. It aimed to defend the sovereignty and territorial integrity of its members and to rid Africa of colonialism, while promoting international co-operation.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The OAU's main task of ending colonialism was nearly complete, and it had been unable to stop wars, dictatorships and genocide because of its rule of non-interference. Study the sources and answer the questions.

**Source A** — a speech by a fictional African foreign minister at an OAU summit, 1964 (invented for this question)

> We have no wish to see our borders redrawn, for that would be a road to endless wars. Let each state keep the frontiers it received, and let us unite to remove the last colonial regimes from our continent.

**Source B** — an editorial in a fictional African newspaper, 1995 (invented for this question)

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The sources agree that the OAU's great purpose was to end colonialism. They differ in emphasis. Source A, a minister speaking at the start, is hopeful and stresses unity and respect for borders, while Source B, an editorial written in 1995, criticises the rule of non-interference that stopped the Organisation from acting when governments killed their own citizens. My own knowledge supports both: the OAU helped decolonisation, but it failed to prevent conflicts such as the genocide in Rwanda in 1994.

explanation: Both sources are invented: a minister's speech and a newspaper editorial.

stem: To what extent was the Organisation of African Unity successful between 1963 and 2002?

points.description: Aims: unity, sovereignty, end of colonialism, co-operation
Successes: Liberation Committee and decolonisation, a united voice at the UN, respect for borders, refugee convention and the African Charter, mediation
Failures: no force or money, non-interference, tolerance of dictators, failure in Nigeria, Rwanda, Liberia and Somalia
Change over time and the move to the AU
Supported judgement

levels.descriptor: Developed, well-supported explanation of several relevant factors or arguments, using accurate and specific knowledge, weighing them against each other and against alternative views, with a sustained line of argument and a supported judgement that answers the question.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; limited balance and little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The OAU was successful in its main aim of decolonisation but much less successful in other respects. Its Liberation Committee gave money, training and arms to liberation movements and kept apartheid and colonialism before the UN, and the OAU gave Africa a united voice and respected borders, which limited border wars. It also adopted a refugee convention and the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights. But it had no force and little money, many members did not pay their dues, and its principle of non-interference meant that it could not act in the Nigerian civil war, the civil wars in Liberia and Somalia or the Rwandan genocide, and critics called it a club of presidents. I conclude that the OAU achieved its founding aim of ending colonialism and apartheid, but failed to protect Africans from conflict and misrule, which is why it was replaced by the African Union.

explanation: Credit aims, successes, failures and a supported judgement.
hints: Compare success in decolonisation with failure on internal conflicts.

stem: Assess the importance of the African Union's right to intervene in grave circumstances.

points.description: The provision: Article 4(h) allows intervention in cases of war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity, and Article 30 allows suspension after coups
Importance: a break with the OAU rule of non-interference, a response to Rwanda, a basis for peace operations

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The right to intervene in grave circumstances is an important change from the OAU. Article 4(h) allows intervention in cases of war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity, and the AU can suspend governments that come to power by coups. It was a response to the failure to act in Rwanda and has provided a basis for peace operations in Burundi, Darfur and Somalia. But members are reluctant to give up sovereignty, resources are limited, and the right has been used selectively. I conclude that it is an important principle which has changed the AU's role, but its effect in practice has been limited by politics and money.

explanation: Credit explained provision, limits and a judgement.
hints: Compare the change on paper with action in practice.
